text: x Asteroids (planetoids) are composed mainly of refractory rocky and metallic minerals, with some ice. x Asteroids range in size from hundreds of kilometres across to microscopic. x Ceres (2.77 AU) is the largest asteroid (946 km in diameter), a protoplanet, and a dwarf planet. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 115 Comets x A comet is an icy small Solar System body that, when passing close to the Sun, heats up due to the effects of solar radiation and the solar wind upon the nucleus and begins to outgas, displaying a visible atmosphere or coma, and sometimes also a tail. x Comets have highly elliptical orbits, unlike the planets which have near-circular orbits. x They are made of frozen gases (water, NH3, CH4, CO2) which hold together rocky and metallic minerals. x Short-period comets (orbital period of a few hundred years) originate in the Kuiper belt or its associated scattered disc, which lie beyond the orbit of Neptune. x Longer period comets, with orbits of thousands of years, come from the more distant Oort Cloud. Halley’s Comet x One of the larger comets is the Halley’s Comet. x The orbit of Halley’s Comet brings it close to the Earth every 76 years ― short-period comet. x It last visited in 1986 and is projected to return in 2061. Kuiper belt x The Kuiper belt is a great ring of debris similar to the asteroid belt but consisting mainly of objects composed primarily of ice. x It extends between 30 and 50 AU from the Sun. Oort Cloud x Oort cloud is a giant shell of icy bodies that encircle the solar system occupying space at a distance between 5,000 and 100,000 AU. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 116 Distance from Sun (NASA / JPL-Caltech, via Wikimedia Commons) Potentially Hazardous Objects (PHO) x They are NEOs (asteroids or comets) that come threateningly close to Earth and large enough to cause sig- nificant regional damage in the event of impact. x All asteroids with a Minimum Orbit Intersection Distance (MOID) of 0.05 AU (7,480,000 km) or less are con- sidered Potentially Hazardous Asteroids (PHAs). x MOID is the minimum distance between two almost overlapping elliptical orbits. x NASA tracks and characterizes NEOs that are 140 meter or larger in size. x However, no asteroid larger than 140 m has a “significant” chance of hitting the Earth for the next 100 years. Meteoroid, Meteor and Meteorite x A meteoroid is any solid debris originating from asteroids, comets or other celestial object and floats through interplanetary space. x A meteor is the streak of light that appears in the sky when a meteoroid enters the atmosphere (mesosphere) at about 200 km at high speed and burns up because of the friction. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 117 x In some cases, the meteoroid does not burn up completely and makes its way to the Earth’s surface. x The surviving chunk is called a meteorite. x The depression created on the earth’s surface after the meteorite’s impact is called as a meteorite crater. Chicxulub crater x Chicxulub crater (Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula) was caused by a meteorite impact that is believed to have wiped out the dinosaurs (5th mass extinction at the end of the Cretaceous 65 million years ago). The devastation potential of a 10 km asteroid (meteorite) x An asteroid roughly 10 km across and travelling at a speed of 20 km/s hit Earth about 65 million years ago. x This impact made a huge explosion and a crater about 180 km across (E = mc2 Î more speed = more energy). x Debris layer in the atmosphere blocked sunlight for months and led to impact winters that lasted for years, leading to the extinction of roughly 3/4 of species that existed at that time, including the dinosaurs. x Tiny mammals that lived in burrows survived. Hence mammals replaced giant reptiles after the impact. x Many asteroids of this type cross Earth's orbit every now and then. x Some of these could potentially hit Earth in the future. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 118 Asteroid Impact Deflection Assessment (AIDA) x There are around 25,000 near-Earth objects (NEOs – asteroids, comets, space debris) that orbit the Sun on a trajectory that brings them close to our planet’s orbit. x According to NASA, as of now, there are about 900 near-Earth objects measuring more than 1 km. x An impact from one of these NEOs can bring devastating effects to Earth. x The latest of the five mass extinctions, Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction (66 million years ago, the end of dinosaurs), is said to have caused by an asteroid or a comet impact. x Over the years, scientists have suggested different ways to ward off asteroid impact threats, such as blowing up the asteroid before it reaches Earth or deflecting it off its Earth-bound course by hitting it with a spacecraft. x Now, scientists have embarked on a plan to test their expertise with the second of these two methods. Asteroid Impact Deflection Assessment x The AIDA is a double-spacecraft kinetic impact mission being developed by NASA ad ESA. x The project aims to study the effectiveness of an impact to ward off an impending asteroid threat. x Th aim of the mission is to test if the technique of deflecting asteroids off their earth-bound course is effective in warding off future asteroid impact threats. x AIDA includes NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) and the ESA’s Hera. Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) x NASA aims to launch DART spacecrafts in 2021. x DART will be put to test on the Didymos binary near-Earth asteroid system. x Didymos binary system consists of Didymos A (about 780 metres in size), and Didymos B (about 160 metres). x The Didymos B will have a distant approach to Earth in 2022, and then again in 2024. x DART adopts kinetic impactor technique to deflect the orbit of the smaller body through an impact by one of the spacecrafts with the target at 6.6 km/s. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 119 x Mission Hera will launch in 2024 and will arrive at the Didymos system in 2027 to measure the impact crater produced by the DART collision and study the change in the asteroid’s orbital trajectory. x The effect of the collision is also monitored by earth based observatories. x Based on the observations, the capabilities of kinetic impact as an asteroid mitigation strategy will be deter- mined. Superhabitable Planets What are Exoplanets? x The word planet is a general term that describes any celestial body that moves around a star. x There are also “rogue” planets that do not orbit stars. x An exoplanet is a planet outside our solar system. x It is an extrasolar planet. What is Dark Energy? x In 1998, it was discovered that the universe is expanding & that this expansion was gaining speed or accel- erating. x There had to be an “invisible” energy that was driving this. x Calculations showed that this dark energy – so called because it did not interact with the observed mass – makes up about 70% of the universe. x It is distributed evenly throughout the universe, not only in space but also in time – in other words, its effect is not diluted as the universe expands. x The even distribution means that dark energy does not have any local gravitational effects, but rather a global effect on the universe as a whole. x This leads to a repulsive force, which tends to accelerate the expansion of the universe. x The rate of expansion & its acceleration can be measured by observations based on the Hubble law. x These measurements, together with other scientific data, have confirmed the existence of dark energy & provide an estimate of just how much of this mysterious substance exists. Dark Matter x The velocity of rotation for spiral galaxies depends on the amount of mass contained in them. x But the outer arms of the Milky Way are rotating much too fast to be consistent with the amount of matter that we know exists in them. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 120 x Such fast rotation is possible only when there is more mass, & that extra mass is believed to come from the dark matter. x Dark matter is a hypothetical form of matter that is thought to account for approximately 85% of the matter in the universe. x Dark energy plus dark matter constitutes 95.1% of the total content of the universe (the rest in the normal matter). In short, we are unsure about what’s there in 95% of the universe! x The majority of dark matter is thought to be composed of some as-yet-undiscovered subatomic particles. x The name dark matter refers to the fact that it does not appear to interact with observable electromag- netic radiation, such as light. x It is thus invisible (or ‘dark’) to the entire electromagnetic spectrum, making it extremely difficult to detect. x Dark matter interacts with the rest of the universe only through its gravity (that’s how we know it exists). Superhabitable Planet x A superhabitable planet is a hypothetical type of exoplanet or exomoon that may be better suited than Earth for the emergence & evolution of life. x The concept was introduced in 2014 by René Heller & John Armstrong, who have criticized the language used in the search for habitable planets, so they propose clarifications because a circumstellar habitable zone (HZ) is not enough to define a planet's habitability x They define a superhabitable world as a terrestrial planet or moon that could support more diverse flora & fauna than there are on Earth, as it would empirically show that its environment is more hospitable to life. x Related term – Goldilocks zone 9 The Goldilocks Zone refers to the habitable zone around a star where the temperature is just right - not too hot & not too cold - for liquid water to exist on a planet. 9 Liquid water is essential for life as we know it. 9 Where we find liquid water on Earth, we also find life. 9 The location of a Goldilocks Zone around another star depends on the type of star. 9 Bigger hotter stars have their Goldilocks Zones further out, while smaller cooler stars such as M-type red dwarf stars have habitable zones much closer in. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 121 Source & Credits Biotechnology Related Concepts Bioweapons x Biological weapons are microorganisms like virus, bacteria, fungi, or other toxins that are produced and released deliberately to cause disease and death in humans, animals or plants. x Biological agents, like anthrax, botulinum toxin and plague can pose a difficult public health challenge. x Bioterrorism attacks could result in an epidemic, for example if Ebola virus was used as biological agents. x Biological weapons are a subset of a larger class of weapons referred to as weapons of mass destruction, which also includes chemical, nuclear and radiological weapons. Bacillus Anthracis (Anthrax) x Bacillus anthracis bacteria, which causes anthrax, is one of the deadliest agents to be used as a biological weapon. x Anthrax has been used as a bioweapon for about a century mixed with powders, sprays, food and water. x The invisible, infectious, odourless and tasteless spores make Anthrax a flexible bioweapon. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 122 Australia Group x The Australia Group (AG) is an informal forum/voluntary group of countries. x The Australia Group is a multilateral export control regime (MECR). x Members, through the harmonisation of export controls, seeks to ensure that exports do not contribute to the development of chemical or biological weapons (CBW) by states or terrorist groups. x The AG at present consists of 42 countries and the European Union. x India formally became the 43rd member. x Australia manages the secretariat. Multilateral Export Control Regime (MECR) x It is an informal group of like-minded supplier countries that seek to contribute to the: 9 Non-proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, 9 Delivery systems, and 9 Advanced conventional weapons through national implementation of guidelines and control lists for ex- ports. x There are currently four such regimes: 1. The Wassenaar Arrangement (WA) on Export Controls for Conventional Arms and Dual-Use Goods and Technologies (It has 42 member). 2. The Nuclear Suppliers Group (NSG), for the control of nuclear related technology (It has 48 partici- pating governments, India is not a member of the NSG). 3. The Australia Group (AG) for the control of chemical and biological technology that could be weaponized. 4. The Missile Technology Control Regime (MTCR) for the control of rockets and other aerial vehicles capable of delivering weapons of mass destruction. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 123 IndiGen: India’s Genome Sequencing Project x The Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) concluded the six-month long exercise of conducting a “whole-genome sequence” of a 1,008 Indians that beloged to diverse ethnicities. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 124 x The project is part of a programme called “IndiGen” and is a precursor to a much larger exercise funded by the Department of Biotechnology to sequence at least 10,000 Indian genomes. x The project involved the Hyderabad-based Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology (CCMB) and the CSIR-Institute of Genomics and Integrative Biology (IGIB). x Globally, many countries have undertaken genome sequencing of a sample of their citizens to determine unique genetic traits, susceptibility (and resilience) to disease. Key Terms x DNA: hereditary material of most of the living beings. x RNA: hereditary material of some microorganisms (virus). x Genes: specific section of DNA which encodes the synthesis of gene product either RNA or for proteins i.e., it is involved in making RNA (transcription) or proteins (translation). x Chromosome: are thread-like structures located inside the nucleus of animal & plant cells. 9 The DNA is coiled to make thread like structure called chromosomes. 9 Human beings have 46 chromosomes (23 from each parent). 9 Each chromosome is made of protein & a single molecule of deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA). x Genome sequencing: Deciphering the exact order of bases pairs (complete DNA sequence) in an organism's genome. 9 This entails sequencing all of an organism's chromosomal DNA as well as DNA contained in the mitochondria and, for plants, in the chloroplast.
